Lesson four! In lesson three, engine x was running, but you never saw a web page. Today you'll find out why, and fix it with dash p, so you can open the container right in your browser.
Let's start by trying it without dash p.
Start engine x in the background, with the name web, exactly like at the end of lesson three. You've used this command before. Pause the video, type it yourself, then continue.
Here it is: docker run, dash d, dash dash name web, engine x. Docker prints a long I D, and no error. So engine x is running.
Now open localhost port eighty eighty in your browser. Oh no. This site can't be reached. Localhost refused to connect.
Why? A container has its own private network. Engine x listens on port eighty inside the container, but nothing connects your PC to it. Even localhost port eighty fails.
Before we try again, let's stop and delete the web container. There are two ways to do it.
Way one uses two commands. First, stop the web container. You've done this before. Pause the video, type it yourself, then continue.
docker stop web. Docker prints the name, and the container is stopped.
Now delete it. Pause the video, type it yourself, then continue.
docker rm web. The container is deleted.
Way two is a shortcut: docker R M, dash f, web. Dash f means force. It stops the container if it's running, then deletes it, all in one command.
Use one way or the other, not both. Once it's deleted, there's nothing left to delete.
Now the right way. Same command, plus dash p, eighty eighty colon eighty. Dash p means publish. It connects a port on your PC to a port inside the container.
Here's the full command: docker run, dash d, dash dash name web, dash p, eighty eighty colon eighty, engine x. We get a long container I D, and no error.
Let's split dash p apart. Eighty eighty is the port on your PC, and you choose it. Eighty is the port inside the container, where engine x listens. That one is fixed.
Now there's a line from port eighty eighty on your PC, to port eighty in the container. Remember, the order is always your PC first, then the container.
But what if you get an error that says, port is already allocated?
You run the same command, and Docker complains. Bind for port eighty eighty failed, port is already allocated. That's a little disappointing.
The rule is: one port, one program. Something else on your PC, maybe another container, already uses port eighty eighty. Only one program can use a host port at a time.
The fix is easy. Delete the new container with docker R M web, and pick another host port, like dash p, eighty eighty one colon eighty. Then open localhost port eighty eighty one.
Let's check the port from the terminal.
List the running containers, then look at the PORTS column. You know this command. Pause the video, type it yourself, then continue.
It's docker P S. Our web container is up, and the PORTS column has something new.
In lesson three, this column said only eighty slash T C P. Now it shows the connection: port eighty eighty on your PC, arrow, port eighty in the container.
And the part with the square brackets is the same thing, for I P version six.
Now the exciting part. Open localhost port eighty eighty again, or just reload the tab.
Welcome to engine x! The page loads. Your browser sends a request to port eighty eighty, and the page comes back.
This page comes from engine x, running inside the container. You did it!
You can also check it from the terminal. curl, localhost port eighty eighty, prints the page's H T M L. There's the title, Welcome to engine x.

Stop the container, then reload the browser tab. Pause the video, type it yourself, then continue.
docker stop web. And after you reload, the page is gone again. This site can't be reached.
Now delete it. Pause the video, type it yourself, then continue.
docker rm web. The container is deleted.
Check that it's gone from all containers, including stopped ones. Pause the video, type it yourself, then continue.
docker P S, dash a. Only the header row, so there are no containers left.
We only removed the container. Now check the image, and list only the engine x image. Pause the video, type it yourself, then continue.
docker image L S, engine x. The image is still there. Keep it, because we need it in the next lessons.
